title: Exposure to untrustworthy websites in the 2016 US election
screen_reason: Individual-level web-traffic study: passively recorded URL-level browsing from the YouGov Pulse panel (7 October - 14 November 2016) merged with survey data, weighted to US adults. It reports (i) the weighted share of Americans who visited at least one untrustworthy website at least once (behavioural REACH), (ii) the mean share of the hard-news information diet accounted for by those websites (EXPOSURE, diet share), and (iii) a verbatim CONCENTRATION statement giving both the group size and its share of traffic. Untrustworthy websites are defined by a peer-reviewed source-reliability list (Grinberg et al. black/orange/red), which is an eligible ground truth under the source-level branch of the inclusion rule.

estimates.measure_type: % of American adults who visited at least one article on an untrustworthy website during the final weeks of the 2016 campaign
estimates.denominator: 2,525 YouGov Pulse panel members with page-level laptop/desktop traffic data, survey-weighted to represent US adults aged 18 and older
estimates.definition: At least one page view, during 7 October - 14 November 2016, of an article on a domain classified black, orange or red by Grinberg et al.
estimates.misinfo_def: "websites that publish factually dubious content, which is often described as fake news"; operationally, websites that "lack the news media's editorial norms and processes for ensuring the accuracy and credibility of information"
estimates.source_quote: We estimate that 44.3% of Americans aged 18 or older visited an article on an untrustworthy website during our study period, which covered the final weeks of the 2016 election campaign (95% CI = 40.8-47.7%).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Total consumption of untrustworthy websites', first paragraph
estimates.ground_truth_detail: 490 domains taken from Grinberg et al. (Science 2019): black (382 sites, 'previously identified by journalists and fact checkers as notable publishers of false or misleading content'), orange (47, 'negligent or deceptive') and red (61, 'little regard for the truth'), the latter two assigned by human review of website editorial practices among sites fact-checked by Snopes or frequently mentioned in Grinberg et al.'s Twitter data. The authors validate the list against professional fact checks and report that 'more than 93% of articles from any of the three untrustworthy categories (black, red and orange) were determined to be false'. Robustness checks in the SI use the Allcott and Gentzkow domain list and a fact-checked-article-level measure.
estimates.moderator_quote: Time-stamped URL-level web traffic data were recorded between 7 October and 14 November 2016. ... Here we focused on data from the 2,525 survey respondents for whom page-level online traffic data from laptop or desktop computers are also available.
estimates.notes: Desktop/laptop browser traffic only. Mobile traffic was excluded from the main text (available for 19% of respondents, n = 629, and without full URLs) and Facebook in-feed content could not be observed because of API restrictions, so this is a floor on true reach. denom_scope = population per the REACH rule (the denominator is the panel/population, not a topic corpus).

estimates.measure_type: mean % of an American's hard-news article consumption that came from untrustworthy websites
estimates.value_raw: an average of 5.9% of all of the articles that Americans read on websites that focused on hard-news topics (95% CI = 5.1-6.7%)
estimates.denominator: Each respondent's total article page views on untrustworthy websites plus page views on domains a topic model classified as focusing on national news, politics or world affairs (Bakshy et al., excluding Amazon, Twitter and YouTube); individual shares averaged with survey weights, respondents with no such visits excluded
estimates.definition: Page views on domains classified black, orange or red by Grinberg et al., as a fraction of that respondent's hard-news page views plus untrustworthy page views
estimates.misinfo_def: "websites that publish factually dubious content, which is often described as fake news"; operationally, websites that "lack the news media's editorial norms and processes for ensuring the accuracy and credibility of information"
estimates.n: articles read by 2,525 panel members (denominator is the pooled hard-news + untrustworthy page views; the exact n for the overall diet mean is not stated in the main text)
estimates.source_quote: In total, articles on these factually dubious websites represented an average of 5.9% of all of the articles that Americans read on websites that focused on hard-news topics during this period
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Total consumption of untrustworthy websites', first paragraph
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same Grinberg et al. black (382) / orange (47) / red (61) domain list as the reach row; validated against professional fact checks, with more than 93% of articles from those categories determined false. The diet denominator uses the Bakshy et al. topic-model classification of hard-news domains.
estimates.moderator_quote: Finally, we measured respondent consumption of hard-news websites classified by a topic model as focusing on national news, politics or world affairs. We summed this measure with total consumption of untrustworthy websites as defined above to construct the denominator for the estimated proportion of the news and information diet of people that comes from untrustworthy websites.
estimates.notes: This is a share of the HARD-NEWS diet, not of all browsing, so it is much larger than the corresponding share of total web activity would be; the abstract rounds it to 'approximately 6%'. The two figures the paper gives by source slant (untrustworthy conservative 4.6%, untrustworthy liberal 0.6%) do not sum to 5.9% because some untrustworthy domains are unclassified for slant, so they are not a clean partition and are recorded in missed_or_uncertain rather than as rows. Respondents with no hard-news or untrustworthy visits are excluded from the denominator, which inflates the mean slightly relative to a whole-population average.

estimates.measure_type: share of all page-level traffic to untrustworthy websites accounted for by the 20% of news consumers with the most conservative information diets
estimates.value_raw: "62% of all page-level traffic to untrustworthy websites ... came from the 20% of news consumers with the most conservative information diets"
estimates.conc_group_label: The 20% of news consumers with the most conservative information diets (top two deciles of average media-diet slant)
estimates.denominator: All page-level visits to untrustworthy websites observed in the YouGov Pulse laptop/desktop traffic, 7 October - 14 November 2016; group denominator is the panel divided into ten equally sized media-diet slant deciles
estimates.definition: Page views on Grinberg et al. black/orange/red domains, attributed to respondents grouped by the pageview-weighted mean ideological slant of the websites they visit (slant from Bakshy et al., based on differential Facebook sharing by self-identified liberals versus conservatives)
estimates.misinfo_def: "websites that publish factually dubious content, which is often described as fake news"; operationally, websites that "lack the news media's editorial norms and processes for ensuring the accuracy and credibility of information"
estimates.n: top 20% of the media-diet-slant distribution (deciles 9-10); slant deciles computed for 2,422 panel members per Fig. 2
estimates.source_quote: In total, 62% of all page-level traffic to untrustworthy websites observed in our data during the study period came from the 20% of news consumers with the most conservative information diets.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Selective exposure to untrustworthy websites', final sentence of the deciles paragraph
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same Grinberg et al. black/orange/red domain list; group membership defined by the Bakshy et al. website-slant score, not by self-reported ideology.
estimates.moderator_quote: We then divided our sample into ten equally sized groups (deciles) ranging from the 10% of respondents with the most liberal information diets to the 10% with the most conservative information diets.
estimates.notes: R1 satisfied: both halves are stated verbatim in a single sentence (group = top 20% of users, share = 62% of untrustworthy traffic). The grouping variable is diet slant, not prior misinformation consumption, so this is concentration among an ideologically defined heavy-consumer group rather than a pure top-N-by-exposure statistic; the discussion restates it as 'echo chambers are deep ... but they are also narrow (the group in question represents only 20% of the public)'.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT EXTRACTED as rows, with the verbatim numbers so an adjudicator can add them. (1) Diet share by source slant: 'articles on untrustworthy conservative websites represented 4.6% of people's news diets (95% CI = 3.8-5.3%) compared with only 0.6% for liberal websites (95% CI = 0.5-0.8%)'. Left out because slant is not a veracity variant and 4.6 + 0.6 does not reconcile with the 5.9% headline (some untrustworthy domains carry no slant classification), so treating them as a partition would be wrong. (2) Party subgroups, which the paper does treat as headline: 'Among Trump supporters, 56.7% read at least one article from an untrustworthy conservative website (95% CI = 51.7-61.8%) compared with 27.7% of Clinton supporters (95% CI = 23.1-32.4%)'; and for untrustworthy liberal websites, Clinton supporters 23.0% (18.8-27.2) versus Trump supporters 10.7% (8.1-13.3). Diet-share counterparts: untrustworthy conservative websites were 11.0% of Trump supporters' news diet (9.2-12.8) versus 0.8% of Clinton supporters' (0.6-1.1); untrustworthy liberal 1.1% for Clinton supporters (0.7-1.5) versus 0.4% for Trump supporters (0.2-0.6). These are subgroup-by-party rows AND slant-restricted at the same time, so they are not comparable with the 44.3%/5.9% headline; I applied the 'keep the main figure' rule. (3) Decile detail that could support additional concentration or intensity rows: reach of untrustworthy conservative websites 'ranges inconsistently from 31% to 48% across the first eight deciles', rising to 59.6% (48.4-70.9) in decile 9 and 84.0% (75.2-92.8) in decile 10; diet share 18.1% (14.1-22.1) in decile 9 and 20.9% (16.6-25.3) in decile 10 versus '0.3-6.2% across the eight remaining deciles'; per-capita intensity 'an average of 25 and 91 articles, respectively' for deciles 9 and 10, and '52 articles from untrustworthy conservative websites on average' in the top 20% (a value_kind per_capita_intensity row if wanted). All are subgroup and slant-restricted. (4) Facebook-usage terciles (Clinton supporters 16.5% / 24.8% / 45.7%; Trump supporters 39.6% / 51.5% / 74.4% visiting untrustworthy conservative sites) and hard-news terciles among Trump supporters (30.9% / 67.0% / 79.8%) are covariate subgroups, not prevalence. (5) NOT ELIGIBLE, computed inside the misinformation-only sample rather than measuring its prevalence: referrer shares -- Facebook appeared among the previous three URLs within 30 s for 15.1% of untrustworthy-website articles versus 5.9% of hard-news articles, Google 3.3% versus 6.2%, Twitter 1.0% versus 1.5%, webmail 9.5% versus 5.4%; and dwell times (64.2 s on untrustworthy articles, 42.1 s hard news, 24.2 s other). (6) NOT ELIGIBLE, fact-checking outcomes rather than misinformation exposure: 25.3% (22.5-28.2) visited a national fact-checking article at least once; 18.6% (16.1-21.1) of Americans both visited an untrustworthy website and saw a fact check, with the Fig. 5 partition 25.7% / 49.0% / 6.7%; and 3 of 111 respondents (2.7%) who read a fact-checkable untrustworthy article also read the matching fact check -- that last one is a within-misinformation figure. (7) VALIDATION FIGURE, not a prevalence estimate: 'more than 93% of articles from any of the three untrustworthy categories (black, red and orange) were determined to be false' -- this is content falsity computed inside a misinformation-only sample (R3 territory), and it is reported without a denominator, so I did not create a within_misinfo_content row. (8) Sample-description numbers that are not misinformation shares: 88% visited a Facebook URL at least once, 76% more than ten times, 56.6% validated turnout, 89% of the most conservative decile preferring Trump, and the ANES/Pulse demographic comparisons in Table 3. DENOMINATOR NOTE: the exact n behind the overall 5.9% diet mean is not printed in the main text; Fig. 1b gives n = 2,016 for the Clinton/Trump supporter subset and Fig. 2b n = 2,334 for those with computable slant, both after excluding respondents with no qualifying visits. Also note the study covers desktop/laptop browsers only, excludes mobile and in-feed Facebook content, and Table 2's models use a shorter traffic window (7-21 October 2016) than the descriptive estimates.

rob.design: Passive URL-level web-traffic metering (YouGov Pulse browser software, all installed desktop/laptop browsers, passwords and financial transactions excluded) for 7 October - 14 November 2016, linked to an online YouGov survey fielded 21-31 October 2016, with validated turnout appended from the TargetSmart voter file and CRT scores from other YouGov surveys. 3,251 survey respondents; the analytic sample is the 2,525 with page-level laptop/desktop traffic; sample size set by budget rather than power analysis; survey weights used throughout to approximate US adults, and the weighted sample is benchmarked against the 2016 ANES face-to-face survey (Table 3). The authors are explicit about non-representativeness: opt-in Pulse panel, people with less than a high school degree underrepresented, a Democratic tilt (42% Clinton vs 33% Trump), presumably 100% home internet access versus 89% in ANES, and higher Facebook usage than the public. Measurement is at DOMAIN level using an external peer-reviewed list (Grinberg et al. black/orange/red, 490 sites) rather than article-level fact-checking, validated by the authors as more than 93% of articles false; robustness checks use the Allcott and Gentzkow list and a fact-checked-article measure. Mobile traffic (19% of respondents) and Facebook in-feed content are unobserved, so exposure estimates are floors. No intercoder reliability applies, since the classification is imported. Analyses are OLS with survey weights; the authors state they did not formally test OLS assumptions. Data and replication code are deposited on Dataverse; IRB approvals at NYU and Dartmouth with informed consent.
rob.item6_quote: The qualifying untrustworthy websites considered in this study are those classified as black (382 websites), orange (47 websites) and red (61 websites) by Grinberg et al.35 The black websites were those that were previously identified by journalists and fact checkers as notable publishers of false or misleading content.
rob.item10_quote: We estimate that 44.3% of Americans aged 18 or older visited an article on an untrustworthy website during our study period, which covered the final weeks of the 2016 election campaign (95% CI = 40.8-47.7%). In total, articles on these factually dubious websites represented an average of 5.9% of all of the articles that Americans read on websites that focused on hard-news topics during this period (95% CI = 5.1-6.7%).
